howItWorks.intro: The calculator runs the same per-mile math dispatchers and fuel desks use, then scales it across your actual operating pattern.
rules: Cost per mile = diesel price per gallon ÷ vehicle MPG
Daily fuel cost = cost per mile × daily miles
Weekly fuel cost = daily fuel cost × days per week
Monthly and annual totals extrapolate the weekly figure across roughly 4.33 weeks per month and 52 weeks per year
howItWorks.outro: These are pump-price, point-in-time figures. They don't account for idle-time burn, state-to-state fuel-tax differences, or a fuel surcharge you may already be collecting from a shipper — add those separately for a true landed cost per mile.

faq.question: What's a realistic MPG for a loaded semi truck?
faq.answer: A loaded Class 8 tractor-trailer typically averages 6 to 8 MPG on the highway. Empty or lightly loaded runs can reach 8-9 MPG, while mountainous terrain, strong headwinds, or an underinflated tire can drop it to 5-5.5 MPG. Aerodynamic trailer skirts and consistent tire pressure can realistically add 0.3-0.5 MPG back.

faq.question: How much does a $0.50/gallon diesel price jump cost per mile?
faq.answer: At 6.5 MPG, a $0.50/gallon increase adds about $0.077 per mile ($0.50 ÷ 6.5). For a truck running 11,000 miles in a month, that's roughly $847 in added fuel cost with no change to the freight rate — which is exactly the gap a fuel surcharge is meant to close.

faq.question: How do carriers calculate fuel surcharges?
faq.answer: Most carriers index their fuel surcharge to the weekly U.S. average diesel price published by the EIA, compared against a baseline price built into the base linehaul rate. The difference is divided by an assumed MPG — often 6 MPG — to produce a cents-per-mile surcharge added to the rate and typically recalculated every week as diesel prices move.

faq.question: Why is diesel usually priced higher than gasoline?
faq.answer: Diesel carries a federal excise tax about 6 cents per gallon higher than gasoline, and diesel demand competes with heating oil during winter months, which can tighten refining supply and push prices up seasonally even when crude oil is flat. Diesel also requires more tightly refined, higher-cetane fuel, which adds production cost.

faq.question: How much fuel does idling burn?
faq.answer: A diesel engine idling to run climate control or cab accessories burns roughly 0.8 to 1 gallon per hour while covering zero miles. Two hours of nightly idling adds 1.6-2 gallons a day — at $3.80/gal, that's $6-7.60 burned before the truck ever moves, or $180-230 over a month.

faq.question: Is fuel cost per mile the same for an owner-operator and a fleet?
faq.answer: No. For an owner-operator, fuel is usually the single largest variable cost, often 20-25% of per-mile revenue — ahead of maintenance, insurance, and tires. A fleet reports a blended average across many tractors, lanes, and driving habits, so a healthy fleet-wide number can still hide individual trucks running well above it.

sections.title: What This Calculator Measures
sections.body: Diesel fuel cost per mile is the number that connects what you pay at the pump to what it costs to move a load one mile down the highway. Enter your diesel price per gallon, your truck's MPG, and your daily mileage, and the calculator divides price by fuel economy to get a per-mile cost, then carries that across your daily, weekly, monthly, and annual totals. A loaded Class 8 tractor-trailer typically returns 6 to 8 MPG on the highway, depending on gross weight, trailer aerodynamics, and terrain — well below what a straight truck or box truck sees, and far below any passenger vehicle. That gap is why fuel is tracked line by line in trucking: it moves margin faster than almost any other cost on the sheet.

sections.title: A Worked Example: $3.80 Diesel at 6.5 MPG
sections.body: Say your truck is averaging 6.5 MPG loaded and diesel is running $3.80 per gallon at the pump. Cost per mile = $3.80 ÷ 6.5 ≈ $0.58 per mile. Run that truck 11,000 miles in a month — a realistic over-the-road total for a solo driver — and fuel alone costs about $6,431 for the month (11,000 × $0.5846). Now drop the MPG to 5.5 because of a headwind-heavy lane, a few underinflated tires, or a heavier load: the same diesel price pushes cost per mile to roughly $0.69, adding about $1,320 to that same 11,000 miles with no change in the rate you're paid. A one-MPG swing at today's diesel prices is worth real money before a truck even sees a maintenance bill or a toll receipt.

sections.title: Owner-Operator Math vs. Fleet Averages
sections.body: For an owner-operator, fuel is usually the largest single variable cost on the P&L — often 20-25% of gross revenue per mile, ahead of maintenance, insurance, and tires combined. A fleet, by contrast, blends cost per mile across dozens or hundreds of tractors and lane mixes, so the figure in a quarterly report is an average that can hide real variance between a driver idling two hours a night for cab heat and one running an auxiliary power unit. Idle time matters more than it looks on a miles-based sheet: a diesel engine idling burns roughly 0.8 to 1 gallon per hour while covering zero miles, so two hours a night adds 1.6-2 gallons a day — at $3.80/gal, that's $6-7.60 burned before the truck turns a wheel. Fuel surcharges exist to pass some of this volatility to shippers: carriers typically index a cents-per-mile surcharge to the weekly U.S. average diesel price against a baseline MPG assumption, often 6 MPG, and recalculate it weekly as prices move. Diesel is volatile in a different way than gasoline, too — it tracks crude oil but also competes with heating oil demand each winter and carries a federal tax about 6 cents higher per gallon, so the retail spread between the two fuels can widen seasonally even when crude holds steady.

howToSteps.title: Enter Your Diesel Price ($/gal)
howToSteps.description: Use the price you're actually paying at the pump or on a fuel card statement, not a regional average — even a 20-cent swing changes the per-mile result.

howToSteps.title: Fill In Vehicle MPG and Mileage
howToSteps.description: Enter your truck's loaded MPG (commonly 6-8 for a Class 8 tractor-trailer), then your typical daily miles and days per week. Pull these from your ECM or fuel logs rather than a manufacturer spec sheet for a realistic number.

howToSteps.title: Click Calculate
howToSteps.description: The calculator divides diesel price by MPG to get cost per mile, then multiplies that across your daily, weekly, monthly, and annual mileage.

howToSteps.title: Review Cost Per Mile Against Your Rate
howToSteps.description: Compare the result to your per-mile freight rate or fuel surcharge. If fuel is eating more than a quarter of your rate, it's worth re-checking MPG, idle habits, or routing before the next load.

tips: A one-MPG drop — from underinflated tires, a heavier load, or a headwind-heavy lane — can add $0.08-$0.12 per mile at diesel prices near $3.80-$4.00/gal. Re-run the numbers whenever your MPG shifts noticeably.

Track diesel price by the week, not the month. Prices along a corridor can vary 30-50 cents per gallon between truck stops, and that spread moves cost per mile more than most maintenance decisions do.

If you're an owner-operator, weigh the cost-per-mile figure against your per-mile freight rate before accepting a load — fuel is usually the first cost that has to clear before anything else is profit.
Idle time doesn't show up in a miles-based calculation, but it shows up on the fuel bill. Budget roughly 0.8-1 gallon per idle hour if you run the engine overnight for climate control.
Fleet managers: check this at the tractor level, not just the fleet average. A fleet-wide MPG average can mask a handful of trucks burning 15-20% more fuel per mile than the rest.

If a rate confirmation includes a fuel surcharge, check what baseline MPG and diesel price it assumes — many surcharge tables still assume 6 MPG, which understates real cost per mile on heavier loads or mountain lanes.
